$NDX Both the 1997 Nasdaq pullback and the current one happened during periods of high optimism around a major technology wave internet and tech infrastructure in the late ’90s, and AI infrastructure today.

In 1997, the Nasdaq experienced a sharp correction of roughly 12% (with a single-day drop of about 7% on October 27) triggered by the Asian financial crisis. Investors worried that currency turmoil and slower growth in Asia would hurt earnings for U.S. tech companies that depended on the region. The sell-off was relatively short-lived. The market recovered within a couple of months, and the broader bull market driven by internet optimism continued into the late 1990s.

The current pullback (as of mid-November 2026) has followed a similar pattern in size and we had a Nasdaq crash last week (+6% drop in a single day). The Nasdaq Composite peaked near 27,600 on October 6 and fell as much as ~12% by early November, entering correction territory before partially recovering. This time the trigger has been more internal: questions about whether the massive spending on AI data centers, GPUs, and related infrastructure will deliver adequate returns, combined with high valuations in tech and AI-related stocks.

In both cases, the corrections arrived while enthusiasm for a transformative technology remained strong. The 1997 episode proved temporary within a multi-year bull market. Whether the current one follows a similar path will depend on how AI capital spending, execution, and earnings evolve from here. Corrections of this magnitude have been relatively common in the Nasdaq’s history, especially during periods of rapid technological change.

I continue to believe we are in the late 1990s and the big bubble is still coming. Share this with your gurus, many of them probably weren’t even born yet, or were still in school learning 1+1=2, while I was already trading in a broker’s room.

Note : 2026 Nasdaq 100 forward PE: Around 19-23 / 1997 around 24-26 

The truly extreme valuations (Nasdaq multiples well above 40-50, with many individual stocks at 100+) arrived later, in 1999–2000 at the peak of the dot-com bubble. We are too far of any bubble like the dot-com.

A lot of us are down significantly this year. I understand why people want to take a break and just hold on to their long-term positions. If you’re heavily invested in the AI sector then you’re probably down too because the whole sector has been hit over the past month or so.

Anyone who has followed me from the beginning knows my portfolio has always been volatile. I knew that was going to be the case when I started investing because I wasn’t interested in the S&P 500 or ETFs. The difference now is the amount of money involved. When I had £10,000 invested, a 50% loss meant losing £5,000. That’s still a lot of money but it was something I could make back in a few months. Now that I have a six-figure portfolio, losing 50% would be a significant hit to my finances. Replacing that money through work could take me years.

Throughout this year I’ve watched my portfolio move up and down by six figures. I like volatility and I like owning volatile stocks but I don’t like seeing swings of that size in both directions. This time it’s made me rethink how I manage my portfolio.

I’m still a long-term investor and the majority of my money will always be in long-term holdings. I’m not panicking. My focus has always been on that part of my portfolio. With my short-term positions I usually cut losses quickly and move on. With my long-term holdings I’m willing to hold through volatility as long as I still believe in the business.

Without going too deeply into it, there are three things I’m changing going forward.

The first is that I won’t be going all in on one stock. At this point I can’t think of a scenario where I would be comfortable doing that again. I can have strong conviction in a company without letting it account for so much of my portfolio.

The second is that I’ll be taking more profits and keeping some cash available. No stock goes up in a straight line and I don’t want to keep watching large gains disappear without taking anything off the table. Having cash also puts me in a better position to take advantage of sell-offs like this one.

The third is that I’ll be looking at other sectors. I’ll still mainly invest in growth stocks but I want to diversify a little away from AI. It feels like almost any negative headline can trigger a sell-off across the sector right now. There’s already a lot of fear around AI and its impact on jobs, so I expect those headlines to keep coming. I don’t want so much of my portfolio reacting to the same news.

I still want to grow my portfolio and I’m still comfortable taking risks. I just need to manage those risks better now that the amounts involved are much larger. If you’re also down significantly this year, I think it’s worth looking at your allocations, how much cash you keep and whether your approach still suits the amount you now have invested. We’re all going to make mistakes but we need to learn from them and make changes where we need to.

《華爾街日報》剛把底牌全掀了：買不起晶片？輝達直接掏出幾百億美元做財務擔保，硬幫 AI 公司把單子簽下來。

目的就一個：把這幫人死死綁成輝達 GPU 的長期買家。

這套操作把表外承諾的盤子吹到了天上。輝達最新財報白紙黑字寫著，各類承諾與擔保總額直接飆到 5,300 億美元——就在一個季度前，這個數字還只有 1,840 億美元。

公司內部其實有人踩煞車，CFO Colette Kress 當時就一直提出質疑，反覆追問這些擔保到底怎麼定價、輝達真正能拿回什麼。

結果今年 8 月開會時，老黃直接打斷她的話，當眾罵她「像隻被車頭燈照傻的鹿（a deer in the headlights）」。

現在風水輪流轉，老黃走人了，當年被罵的那個 CFO 坐上了臨時 CEO 的位子。

要看懂這顆雷有多大，先看懂這套「AI 資金閉環」是怎麼轉的：   

輝達投錢給 AI 公司，或者幫它的貸款和租賃做擔保。   
這家公司拿著這筆錢和信用去蓋數據中心。  

數據中心裡塞滿輝達的 GPU。   輝達把這批 GPU 算進自己的銷售營收。   

萬一這家公司算力租不出去，輝達還承諾把沒用完的算力買回來。

看明白了嗎？同一筆交易裡，輝達同時當投資人、放款人、供應商，外加接盤俠。錢從輝達口袋掏出去，轉一圈又變成了輝達的營收。

CoreWeave 就是最現成的例子。輝達既持有它的股份、賣晶片給它，還簽約承諾在 2032 年前買下它最多 63 億美元的閒置算力。

盤子最大的是 OpenAI。輝達給它俄亥俄州數據中心提供高達 1,050 億美元的擔保、包辦裡面所有晶片，還順手往承建這座數據中心的公司投了 15 億美元。

大客戶想跑路，上游供應鏈合約又死死鎖著不能退，底下全靠輝達拿信用在幫小客戶續命。

裂縫其實早就炸開了：

新興雲端股這週集體跳水，Nebius 暴跌超過 20%，CoreWeave 盤中最低也砸了 17%。

OpenAI 這輪融資拿到的錢比預期少，估值也縮水了。

But after a sharp market correction and a powerful rebound, the big question remains: is this the beginning of a sustainable recovery or just another oversold bounce?

*

$SPY: V-bottom, W-bottom, or another selloff?

After falling from roughly $781 toward $732, $SPY staged an impressive recovery toward $763. Now the market faces an important test.

Can $SPY hold the $753 area, consolidate, and form a bullish continuation pattern? Or will sellers regain control and force another leg lower?

A shallow retracement would be constructive. A higher-low W-bottom could provide an even stronger foundation for a year-end rally. But losing support would raise the risk of renewed weakness.

*

Technology stocks have experienced significant volatility, with $QQQ dropping from approximately $762 to $647 before rebounding toward $695–$696.

That $695–$696 zone is now immediate resistance, while $679 remains the key support level.

Holding $679 and absorbing selling pressure could set up another advance. Breaking below it would weaken the recovery and potentially open the door to lower prices.

*

Nvidia finally reached an important weekly support area after a steep decline following Jensen Huang's departure. A high-volume hammer reversal attracted buyers, triggering a sharp rebound.

With $NVDA green this morning and approaching the $171 gap-fill area, I believe traders who bought near the lows should consider trimming positions.

A move toward the 8-day moving average is possible, but a short-term bounce doesn't necessarily mean the downtrend is over.

*

$TSLA–$SPCX takeover rumors are heating up. Could Elon Musk combine Tesla and SpaceX?

Speculation surrounding a potential transaction has intensified as Tesla recently traded as high as $422.

I discuss rumors of a possible deal around $420 and suggest that, if a transaction happens, it could come relatively quickly.

However, a $420 valuation would offer little premium at recent prices. Takeover speculation can also backfire if the final terms disappoint investors.

Last week on Thursday, I deployed 25% of my Blood in the Street Account during the correction.

The strategy is systematic: begin buying around 6% below market highs, add exposure near a 10–11% correction, and potentially deploy more capital during a 20% decline.

The subsequent rebound created substantial trading opportunities without requiring me to predict the exact bottom.

Now I am waiting for the new all-time high.

*

So, cooler PPI may help fuel bullish momentum, but the technical picture still needs confirmation. 

Watch $SPY at $753, $QQQ at $679, and whether buyers can push through overhead resistance.

The year-end rally is possible but the market still has to prove it.

Just to state the nuances of my opinion: Jensen is irreplaceable to $NVDA.

No other CEO can visit a chicken shop in Korea, noodle shop in Japan

And rally hundred of billions of capital and supply chain commitment into Nvidia’s next technological vision.

As for Nvidia: the their roadmap is intact, their existing commitment and revenues are still preserved under Jensen’s leadership.

They’ll still be around 5-10 years from now, given how fundamentally important they are to AI supply chains. 

Under a new leader they can still continue growing if AI demand is intact and maintain their current lines.

But I don’t know anyone who can possibly think that under anyone else, whether it’s Tim Cook or an accountant:

That Nvidia could compound 70% capacity constrained growth Y/Y, without a leader like Jensen making these transformational bets.

As for AI implications:

I’m heavily bullish directionally, given AI is the most transformational technology in human history.

- I expect some potential slowdown in Nvidia’s ecosystem.

I don’t think an accountant can make the same aggressive level of commitments to Neoclouds or supply chains in Taiwan, Korea, Japan beyond existing architectures.

Then rally the capital and trust to make it happen.

- I do expect the next CEO to be more politically aligned with Washington in restricting China GPU access

- I also see the next CEO being less supportive of open weight models (positive for OpenAI/Anthropic)

- I’m less optimistic on $NVDA maintaining their competitive advantages against $AMD, $AVGO, and hyperscalers.

One person doesn’t break the AI trade, I expect companies from optics to memory to still outperform.

However, my confidence in the next leg of Nvidia’s growth, beyond their current roadmap, has been shaken without Jensen Huang.

The Cycle Isn’t Over. Demand for Intelligence Has No Human Ceiling

Every past tech cycle ended for the same reason: demand ran out of people. There were only so many households to buy a PC, so many users to get online and so many people to carry a smartphone. Once adoption saturated, capacity caught up, prices broke and the cycle turned.

AI breaks that pattern. Demand for intelligence isn’t capped by human headcount, because machines consume it too. AI agents call other agents, models generate their own training data, and reasoning models burn many times more tokens on every query. Each gain in efficiency becomes more consumption, not spare capacity.

The data shows it:

•  H100 rents are at a record: renting a previous-generation H100 now costs $3.10 an hour, up 56% in a year. In a normal cycle, legacy chips get cheaper as new chips arrive. Blackwell is shipping, yet the H100 still isn’t obsolete, and it’s earning more.

•  Usage is compounding: token volume is up about 40-fold in a year, even as the price per token fell from about $2.00 to $0.80.

•  Inventories are thin: memory makers hold under 10 days of supply.

A cycle ends when supply overtakes demand. Rising prices for old hardware tell you supply is still chasing demand. Wall st. can argue about multiples, but the earnings cycle isn’t over.

I believe Jensen’s resignation could have significant implications for memory companies, particularly their relationship with NVIDIA around NVHBM.

Of course, NVIDIA is unlikely to change its NVHBM roadmap immediately just because Jensen is gone. What I am watching is the influence that persuaded suppliers to commit to that roadmap. In my view, Jensen played a major role in laying out future demand, convincing suppliers to invest ahead of it, and securing favorable pricing and supply allocations. My biggest question is whether his successor can maintain the same level of trust and influence under these circumstances.

Take SK hynix, for example. According to industry research, SK hynix reportedly supplies NVIDIA with HBM at lower prices than it charges NVIDIA’s competitors, even for the same performance bin. Accepting a somewhat lower price still made sense in exchange for substantial volume and long term business opportunities. I believe that relationship also helped SK hynix navigate the recent HBM4 situation.

But what if Jensen’s absence creates more uncertainty around NVIDIA’s execution and growth prospects, while incremental demand shifts toward Google’s and OpenAI’s custom chips or AMD? And what if that demand keeps growing? If memory suppliers can secure sufficient volume and better terms from other customers, wouldn’t they have less reason to offer NVIDIA especially favorable pricing or prioritize it when allocating limited engineering resources and production capacity?

Looking at NVHBM through that lens, I think we could see changes ahead. Consider Samsung. It had to accept what could arguably be seen as a humiliating requirement to use base dies manufactured by TSMC for NVHBM. But if overall AI demand holds up while its customer base diversifies, might Samsung have room to make a different choice?

Of course, none of this is certain, and it remains speculation. Still, I think these potential shifts in the memory industry are worth watching closely. I will continue tracking developments and sharing my insights.

#2.  We don't need traditional marketing automation anymore. That's dead. But we need  agentic marketing

Over the last 60 days we've moved off traditional marketing automation entirely. We still to do marketing.  Our list is 450k+, and we send millions of emails and more.  But it's now done almost entirely agentically.

We don't need templates for emails and promos. 10K has built all those, and we rebuild them dynamically for each send in a way no template ever could. In fact, many of our emails are 100% personalized for real to each recipient, even at mass scale.

And yes, consent is incredibly important, as is deliverability. But you can get that headless from many top tier vendors here. This doesn't lock you in anymore.

I joined @CNBC's The Exchange to discuss what I've been calling Schrödinger's Strait: a Strait that is neither fully open nor fully closed. 

We know that barrels are getting through, keeping the prompt oil market relatively in balance and maintaining prices in the $85–$100 range - but it does nothing to make the next one cheaper.

We need to look beyond whether or not the barrels are passing through the Strait and assess the real issue, which is the extraordinary cost of delivering oil to consumers - a bubbling cauldron of supply and demand  imbalances - shipping, insurance, refining, logistics, any one of which can become the next problem and all of which are combining to ensure the price of delivered barrel of oil is as high as it has been through this entire episode.

That's why I think the war trade in prompt oil has largely played out, but the regime trade remains very much intact.

Bitcoin fell 19% into the biggest IPO ever. Now it's down 18% heading into the second biggest.

SpaceX raised $75B when it went public on June 12. In the 50 days before it listed, Bitcoin dropped 19%. Anthropic plans to raise up to $64B when it lists next week, and Bitcoin is down 18% over the same stretch. Overlay the two and they look almost the same.

What happened after the SpaceX IPO is the notable part. Bitcoin bottomed 18 days after the listing, then recovered all the way. By Day 100, it was above where it started.

Bitcoin around the SpaceX IPO:

Day -50 to IPO day: -19%
Low (Day +18): -25%
Day +50: still -20%
Around Day +70: a sharp rally
Day +100: +3.7%

From the IPO-day close to Day +100, Bitcoin gained 28%. From the low, it gained 39%.

The takeaway is that the selling came in the run-up to the listing. The bottom had effectively happened by the IPO, and the recovery came relatively shortly after, and it came all at once.

If Anthropic follows the same pattern, most of the drawdown is behind us, and it could reverse quickly over the next couple of months. And Bitcoin is sitting right at its 200-week moving average.

Map the SpaceX path onto today's price and you get roughly $90k by late February. Markets rarely follow a comparison like this exactly. But we remain very constructive on both the technicals and the fundamentals heading into 2027, and it's not hard to imagine what the narrative would be if anything close to this plays out.

엔비디아를 제외한 고객사중에는 27년 HBM4로 바로 전환하기보다 HBM3E로 용량과 대역폭을 확대하다가 28년 HBM4를 도입하거나 바로 HBM4E로 점프하는 움직임도 꽤 보임. 앤스로픽은 대놓고 이러한 전략을 공개함.

핵심은 HBM4의 수익성과 범용 DRAM의 공급 부족임.

범용 DRAM 수급이 안정되려면 웨이퍼당 Bit 생산량이 20% 이상 증가하는 D1c 공정 물량이 시장에 유의미하게 공급돼야 하는데, 아무리 빨라도 2027년 중순 이후로 예상됨.

문제는 그때까지 HBM4의 수익성이 범용 DRAM대비 심각할정도로 낮다는것. 실제로 이번 하이닉스와 삼성 영업이익 차이가 많이 좁혀졌는데 삼성이 CAPA 증가물량을 죄다 HBM4에 쏟아부은 영향이라는 얘기도 있음.

HBM은 DRAM 노드가 미세화되더라도 웨이퍼당 실질 Bit 생산량 증가가 매우 적음. 결국 범용 DRAM 대비 낮아지는 생산성을 가격 인상으로 보전해야 하는데, 동일한 이익률을 확보하려면 고객사가 받아들이기 어려운 가격이 형성될 수밖에 없음. 게다가 현재 하닉마이크론은 HBM4 Bit 공급 가능량이 시장 기대치보다 훨씬 낮음.

고객사 입장에서도 HBM4의 가격 부담도  상당하고 공급량도 적기때문에 당장은 HBM3E를 연장하고 2028년 HBM4E 도입 시점에 범용 DRAM 가격 안정화와 함께 가격 협상에 나서는 편이 유리할수도 있음. 추론 서비스 제공자들의 현재 병목은 대역폭보다는 서비스 확대를 위한 DRAM 절대용량이 더 큰 상황이라 무리하게 당장 HBM4로 전환하는건 쉽지 않아보임.

제조사 역시 무리하게 HBM4 공급을 확대하기보다 적정 점유율을 유지하면서 수익성이 높은 범용 DRAM 생산에 더욱 집중할것으로 보임. 

결국 2027년 HBM 공급 부족은 심각할거 같고, HBM3E의 수명은 예상보다 길어질거라고 봄.

Three signs the tide is turning our way

A month ago, India was the market nobody wanted to touch. Today, looks like FIIs can’t get back in fast enough. Funny how quickly the story changes.

We are seeing a possible regime shift over the last week or two. The narrative for FIIs seems to have flipped from ‘Anywhere but India’ to ‘India, the safe haven’. Too early to say if it sustains, but it is a welcome change.

Let me walk you through three signs that the tide may finally be turning our way, and one global risk staring at all of us.

One: The FIIs are coming back

₹60,698 Cr. That is what FPIs have bought in Indian equities in just seven trading days of November. The highest net buying over any seven consecutive trading days since January 2021.

Two: The earnings are strong

Q2 is almost done, and it turned out far better than anyone expected. Remember the backdrop we walked into Q2 with, crude above $100, geopolitical tension, sea routes and logistics disrupted. And still, India Inc delivered.

The median revenue growth for Nifty 50 and NSE 500 stands at 17.4% and 18.6%. Median PAT at 22.3% and 20.4%, as of Nov 10th. Numbers like these, in a quarter like that, tell you something about the quality of these businesses.

Three: The valuations are right

The market went nowhere while earnings kept doing their job, and the result is a market that looks reasonable even after this run-up. Nifty 50 is at a one-year forward PE of around 18x (5Y median 20.8x), Nifty Midcap 150 around 25x (5Y median 30x), Nifty Smallcap 250 at 29x (5Y median 28.3x). 

Broadly, nothing stretched. There is no euphoria out there. If anything, there is still a fair bit of despair.

Coming to our Surge India performance:

Surge India was down -4.1% in Oct 2026, as compared to our primary benchmark Nifty 50 TRI at +1.9% and secondary benchmark Nifty 500 Multicap 50:25:25 TRI at -1.8%.

Surge delivered a strong Q2. The median revenue growth is at 34% YoY, and median PAT growth is at 50.4% (as of Nov 10th).

Our top 3 sectors continue to be Automobiles & Components (21.7%), Capital Goods (20.5%) and Pharmaceuticals (19.7%), and we remain bullish on all three.

To summarise,

After two years of waiting, three things have finally turned our way at the same time, the liquidity is coming back, earnings are strong, and the valuations are still sane. None of them alone means much. Together, they are the best setup we have seen in two years.

Yes, there is a global risk flashing in the background, and we are watching it closely. But you never get a clean setup with zero risk; those don’t exist. You get moments where the odds quietly turn in your favour, and this feels like one of them.

Since January 2026, this figure has surged +490 basis points.

Meanwhile, the spread differential between CCC- and BBB-rated corporate debt has widened to ~1,200 basis points, its widest level in at least 5 years.

This means investors are demanding ~12 percentage points more in compensation to hold the lowest-rated debt rather than first-notch investment-grade corporate bonds.

Cracks are spreading quickly through the lowest-quality credit.

posts.text:
At a separate event on Tuesday evening, Bowman was asked by the Heritage Foundation's E.J. Antoni about how monetary policy could be effective at dealing with today's inflation if it is being driven by an energy supply shock.

Bowman says you can only look through something for so long: "Especially with today's CPI print, it just indicates to me that the time has come, for me anyway, to shift the focus to inflation and trying to lower inflation."

***

ANTONI: So looking at the inflation that we see today, I think it's pretty clear if you look at not just the headline CPI numbers, but then you look at the core numbers, you look at trimmed mean and median, that what we're dealing with is primarily, if not exclusively, an energy shock. And in fact, we saw in those different ways that you can remove out buyers from the index, the inflation readings were continuing to fall until September, and now it's really just the last couple of months that we are seeing energy inflation, if you will, kind of spill out of the gas tank and hit everything else in the broader economy. 

So how does the Fed navigate something like an energy shock that we have today where the problem is not actually a monetary phenomenon, but instead the problem is really a supply shock? And if that's the case, how does that, if at all, change the way you and the Fed more broadly look at how they can use monetary tools to address what looks like a non-monetary problem? 

BOWMAN: EJ, that's a great question. And I address that in my remarks as well because generally with an energy shock, you try to look through that for as long as you can. But because we've been experiencing it for as long as we have, it is, I think over the last few inflation reports, we've seen that the inflation pressures have been broadening. And so we've reached the point where I don't think that you can as obviously look through them, especially as we have a strong labor market and we have a dual mandate, full employment and stable prices. So I think especially with today's CPI print, it just indicates to me that the time has come, for me anyway, to shift the focus to inflation and trying to lower inflation.

October PPI: Wholesale Inflation Implies Rising PPE and December Fed Rate Hike

Wholesale inflation advanced 0.3% in both the headline and core in October, which resulted in a 6.5% increase in the former and a 5% increase in the latter. The September estimate saw an upward revision to 1.4% from 1.3% in the headline number and to 0.8% from 0.7%.

Inflation is broadening as topline increases bleed into the core with a 3-to-4-month lag which has resulted in sharply rising transportation and food costs.

Data from both the CPI and PPI used to estimate the PCE that the Fed utilizes to make policy point towards a 3.8% increase in inflation over the past year and a 3.2% advance in the core. While the November data will look much better due to the recent ease in oil and energy costs it will not provide sufficient relief to policymakers to avoid a December rate hike.

We think that the PPI data and the forward look on the PCE locks in a twenty-five-basis point Fed rate hike as the central bank has fallen behind the curve on inflation.
